# Comparison with In-Process Security Models

Dimension comparing OpenShell's out-of-process enforcement against Claude Code
hooks, Docker, AppArmor/SELinux, gVisor, Firecracker, Kata Containers, AARTS,
and Microsoft Defender.

## Summary Comparison

| Technology | Isolation Depth | Subprocess Coverage | Bypass Resistance | Dev Friction | Performance | Maturity |
|------------|----------------|--------------------|--------------------|-------------|-------------|----------|
| Claude Code Hooks | Application | None | Low (regex evasion) | Low | Negligible | Production |
| OpenShell | Kernel LSM + proxy | Full | High | Medium | Low-moderate | Developer preview |
| Docker (plain) | Process (shared kernel) | Full (within container) | Medium | Low | Minimal | Production |
| AppArmor/SELinux | Kernel LSM | Full | High | High (requires root) | Negligible | Production |
| gVisor | User-space kernel | Full | Very high | Medium | 10-30% I/O [21] | Production |
| Firecracker | Hardware (hypervisor) | Full (dedicated kernel) | Very high | High | ~125ms boot [21] | Production |
| Kata Containers | Hardware (VMM) | Full (dedicated kernel) | Very high | Medium (K8s native) | ~200ms boot [21] | Production |
| AARTS | Application (standardized) | Via host adapter | Depends on engine | Low-medium | Depends on engine | Draft v0.1 [22] |

## Claude Code Hooks vs OpenShell

| Dimension | Claude Code Hooks | OpenShell |
|-----------|------------------|-----------|
| Enforcement layer | Application (Node.js process) | Kernel (Landlock) + Proxy [1][2] |
| Subprocess visibility | None — "once control passes to a subprocess, the application has no visibility" [9] | Full — kernel enforcement covers all processes |
| Bypass via encoding | Regex evasion with shell tricks | Not applicable — syscall/TCP level [3] |
| TOCTOU | Check-then-execute gap | Continuous kernel enforcement [12] |
| Exfiltration | Allowed channels unmonitored | Deny-by-default egress [9]; covert channels remain |
| Config weaponization | Unprotected | Protectable via filesystem policy [9] |
| Developer friction | Low (hooks are fast) | Higher (sandbox creation, policy management) |
| Maturity | Production | "Untested under real-world adversarial conditions" [20] |

## Docker Isolation

Docker provides process-level isolation with shared kernel [21]. OpenShell adds
Landlock, seccomp, and network proxy on top. Docker alone is rated for "Trusted
code only in single-tenant environments" [21]. OpenShell hardens containers but
inherits Docker's shared-kernel weakness: "Vulnerable to kernel exploits enabling
container escape" [21].

## gVisor

gVisor interposes on syscalls via user-space Sentry process, "reducing kernel
attack surface" [21]. Overhead: "10-30% on I/O-heavy workloads" [21]. Provides
stronger isolation than Landlock (user-space kernel vs kernel LSM) at higher
performance cost. For I/O-heavy AI coding agents, the 10-30% overhead is
significant.

## Firecracker MicroVMs

Hardware-enforced isolation with dedicated kernel per workload [21]. "~125ms"
boot time, "<5 MiB" overhead per VM [21]. "Attackers must escape both the guest
kernel and the hypervisor" [21]. Strongest isolation available.

"For production AI agents executing untrusted code: Use Firecracker microVMs or
Kata Containers" [21].

## Kata Containers

Hardware-enforced via VMM with Kubernetes-native CRI [21]. "~200ms" boot [21].
Recommended for "Regulated industries, multi-tenant Kubernetes, zero-trust" [21].
OpenShell could potentially run inside Kata for defense-in-depth, though no
documentation confirms this.

## AARTS Standard

AARTS v0.1 [22] defines 19 hook points with host/adapter/engine architecture:

- **PreToolUse**: Before shell commands, file writes, network requests [22]
- **PreLLMRequest**: Inspects prompt integrity [22]
- **PreSkillLoad/PrePluginLoad**: Supply chain controls [22]
- **PreMCPConnect**: Treats MCP connections as trust boundaries [22]
- **PreMemoryRead/PreMemoryWrite**: Persistent memory protection [22]

Key differences from OpenShell:
- AARTS is an interoperability standard; OpenShell is an enforcement runtime
- AARTS includes application-layer hooks (prompt inspection, skill loading)
  that OpenShell's kernel-layer enforcement cannot cover [22]
- AARTS verdict structure includes confidence scoring and "ask" verdicts [22]
- OpenShell provides enforcement depth that AARTS implementations cannot
  guarantee

**AARTS and OpenShell are complementary, not competitive** [22].

## Cisco AI Defense + OpenShell

Cisco adds governance and verification atop OpenShell's enforcement [17]:

"OpenShell constrains what agents can do. Cisco AI Defense enforces what they
do and verifies what they did" [17].

Three-act model: pre-deployment verification, runtime enforcement, audit-grade
tracing of "every reasoning step, tool call, and decision point" [17].

## Architectural Insight

The consensus across sources is that layered security is required [9][10][22]:
- NVIDIA: "Sanitize where possible, sandbox where necessary" [10]
- AARTS: Tiered conformance levels [22]
- Cisco: Infrastructure constraints + governance verification [17]
- Harang: OS-level enforcement as mandatory, not optional [9]

No single mechanism is sufficient.
